rule.bazi.day_master.jia: Tradition pictures Jia Wood (甲) as a tall tree: upright, strong and growing steadily upward. It is said to flourish with warmth.
rule.bazi.day_master.yi: Tradition pictures Yi Wood (乙) as leaves, flowers and climbing plants: soft and flexible, yet able to work its way through hard ground, and at its best with something to lean on.
rule.bazi.day_master.bing: Tradition pictures Bing Fire (丙) as the blazing sun: fierce, generous and open, unafraid of frost and snow.
rule.bazi.day_master.ding: Tradition pictures Ding Fire (丁) as a lamp flame: gentle on the outside, bright and clear within, burning steadily rather than fiercely.
rule.bazi.day_master.wu: Tradition pictures Wu Earth (戊) as a mountain: solid, weighty, centred and upright, the ground that other things rely on.
rule.bazi.day_master.ji: Tradition pictures Ji Earth (己) as garden soil: humble and moist, centred, quietly storing and nurturing what grows in it.
rule.bazi.day_master.geng: Tradition pictures Geng Metal (庚) as raw iron: tough, direct and strong-willed. It is said to be cleared by Water and sharpened by Fire.
rule.bazi.day_master.xin: Tradition describes Xin Metal (辛) as gentle, warm and clear: a refined and sensitive kind of strength.
rule.bazi.day_master.ren: Tradition pictures Ren Water (壬) as a great river: always moving, firm at its core, flowing around obstacles without standing still.
rule.bazi.day_master.gui: Tradition pictures Gui Water (癸) as rain and dew: the softest water, yet it reaches everywhere and quietly nourishes.
rule.bazi.ten_god.bi_jian: The Friend (比肩) is the same element as you. Tradition reads it as self-reliance, and as peers who stand alongside you.
rule.bazi.ten_god.jie_cai: Rob Wealth (劫财) is a peer star: companions and rivals. The old text speaks of competition among equals over shared resources.
rule.bazi.ten_god.shi_shen: The Eating God (食神) stands for ease, enjoyment and natural expression. The old text links it with a generous, contented nature.
rule.bazi.ten_god.shang_guan: The Hurting Officer (伤官) stands for talent, outspokenness and independence. The old text describes many skills together with a proud streak that questions authority.
rule.bazi.ten_god.pian_cai: Indirect Wealth (偏财) is the second wealth star: resources that come through opportunity and dealings with many people. Tradition adds that one needs the capacity to manage them.
rule.bazi.ten_god.zheng_cai: Direct Wealth (正财) stands for steady, earned resources. The old text stresses having the strength to make use of them: enough at the right time matters more than a great amount.
rule.bazi.ten_god.qi_sha: Seven Killings (七杀) is the traditional name for a demanding, competitive force: pressure, challenge and drive. The old text says it serves well when it is kept under discipline.
rule.bazi.ten_god.zheng_guan: The Direct Officer (正官) stands for rules, duty and recognised standing. The old text calls it a noble star that does best when left undisturbed.
rule.bazi.ten_god.pian_yin: The Indirect Resource (偏印) stands for unconventional learning and an independent mind. The old text cautions that things may be started and left unfinished.
rule.bazi.ten_god.zheng_yin: The Direct Resource (正印) stands for support, learning and protection. The old text links it with thoughtfulness and with help received from elders.

legal.title: How we work
legal.tradition: These are traditional systems of belief. They are not science and they do not predict the future. Fate Tutor shows what each tradition says and where it says it, in the language of tendencies.
legal.offlimits: We do not give readings about death, lifespan, serious illness, accidents or disasters, even where old texts do.
legal.advice: For decisions about health, money, law or marriage, please speak to a qualified professional. A traditional reading is a perspective, not advice.
legal.review: Readings marked “awaiting expert review” follow a named source but have not yet been checked by a practitioner.
legal.privacy: Your birth details stay on your device and are never sent anywhere. So that they carry from page to page, they are kept in this browser tab until you close it. On a tradition page you can choose “Remember on this device” or “Forget my details”.
legal.hosting: This page is delivered by GitHub Pages, and its fonts by Google Fonts. As with any website, those services see your internet address when the page loads. pg.zodiac.about.title: What is the Chinese zodiac?
pg.zodiac.about.p1: The twelve animals (生肖) name the twelve Earthly Branches, an ancient Chinese way of counting years, months and hours. Combined with the ten Heavenly Stems, they make a cycle of sixty years that is still printed on Chinese calendars.
pg.zodiac.about.p2: Popular tradition gives each animal a character. These associations are folk tradition, with no single classical source, and Fate Tutor labels them that way.
pg.zodiac.about.p3: Two calendars give two start dates for the year: Lunar New Year (the popular way) and Start of Spring, 立春 (the way BaZi counts). For most birthdays they agree; for births between late January and mid February they can differ, and this page shows both.

pg.bazi.about.title: What is BaZi?
pg.bazi.about.p1: BaZi (八字, eight characters), also called the Four Pillars, is a Chinese tradition that records the year, month, day and hour of birth in the old sixty-pair calendar. Each pillar is one Heavenly Stem above one Earthly Branch, and each character belongs to one of the five elements: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water.
pg.bazi.about.p2: The classical texts read a chart from the Day Master, the upper character of the day pillar. The pictures of the ten Day Masters on this page follow 滴天髓 (Di Tian Sui), and the names for how other characters relate to the Day Master, the Ten Gods, follow 淵海子平 (Yuan Hai Zi Ping). Each statement shows its source.
pg.bazi.about.p3: Schools differ on a few settings, and Fate Tutor shows them openly: whether the day and hour use the sun's own time at the birthplace or the clock, and whether the day changes at 23:00 or at midnight. Without a birth time the hour pillar is left open rather than guessed.

pg.numerology.about.title: What is numerology?
pg.numerology.about.p1: Numerology as taught today is a modern system, not an ancient one. Its Pythagorean form was set out in the early 20th century, mostly in English-language books. It borrows the name of the Greek thinker Pythagoras, but the method on this page does not come from him or from any ancient text.
pg.numerology.about.p2: Numbers are reduced by adding their digits until one digit is left; 11, 22 and 33 are kept and called master numbers. Teachers differ on the details. This page reduces the month, day and year separately and then adds them, and it also shows the other common method, adding every digit at once, when that gives a different answer.
pg.numerology.about.p3: Name numbers use the 26 Latin letters only: A = 1 to I = 9, then J = 1 again, and Y counts as a consonant. Names written in other scripts belong to other traditions and are not forced into this table. What each number is linked with comes from this modern system; it is not science and not a prediction.

pg.weton.step.4.after: The market week (Legi, Pahing, Pon, Wage, Kliwon) comes round every 5 days. {days} ÷ 5 leaves {rest}, so it moves {rest} on from Legi: {pasaran}.
pg.weton.step.4.before: The market week (Legi, Pahing, Pon, Wage, Kliwon) comes round every 5 days. Going back {days} days lands where going {rest} on from Legi does: {pasaran}.
pg.weton.step.5: Each day and each market day has a value (neptu): {day} {day_neptu} + {pasaran} {pasaran_neptu} = {total}. The weton is {name}.
pg.weton.step.6.evening: The birth was after 18:00. Javanese days begin at sunset, so by that reckoning the birth already belongs to the next day: {name} (neptu {neptu}). Both are shown; ask your family which was used.
pg.weton.step.6.return: Seven days and five market days line up again every 35 days (7 × 5). This weton next comes round on {date}.
pg.weton.about.title: What is a weton?
pg.weton.about.p1: The Javanese calendar runs two weeks side by side: the seven-day week used around the world, and an older five-day week of market days, Legi, Pahing, Pon, Wage and Kliwon, once tied to markets that moved from town to town. Together they make 35 different pairs, and the same pair returns every 35 days. Javanese calendars still print both.
pg.weton.about.p2: Primbon books, such as the Kitab Primbon Betaljemur Adammakna, give each day and each market day a number (neptu) and add them. Tradition uses the totals when comparing two birthdays or choosing a day for an event. Fate Tutor shows the numbers and how they are added, and does not judge any total as better or worse.
pg.weton.about.p3: In Javanese reckoning a new day begins at sunset, not at midnight. Sunset in Java is close to 18:00 all year, so Fate Tutor treats a birth at or after 18:00 on the clock as an evening birth and shows both wetons: the one of the calendar date and the next day's. Families differ on which they use; ask yours.

pg.bazi.pro.ex.god.title: Ten God 十神
pg.bazi.pro.ex.god.what: How a character relates to the Day Master: the same element, the element it produces, the one it controls, the one that controls it, or the one that produces it. Each is split by Yin and Yang into two, giving ten.

pg.bazi.pro.ex.god.src: 淵海子平, the sections on the Ten Gods
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stem.title: Heavenly Stem 天干
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stem.what: The upper character of a pillar: one of ten stems, each with an element and a Yin or Yang side.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stem.how: Year stem from the sixty-year cycle; month stem from the year stem (the Five Tigers rule); day stem from the unbroken sixty-day count; hour stem from the day stem (the Five Rats rule).
pg.bazi.pro.ex.branch.title: Earthly Branch 地支
pg.bazi.pro.ex.branch.what: The lower character of a pillar: one of twelve branches, which are also the twelve zodiac animals.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.branch.how: Year branch from Start of Spring (立春); month branch from the Sun's position; hour branch from the two-hour block of the true sun time.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.hidden.title: Hidden stems 藏干
pg.bazi.pro.ex.hidden.what: Each branch stores one to three stems: a main one (本气) and lesser ones (中气, 余气). A Ten God is worked out for each.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.hidden.how: Looked up from the fixed hidden-stem table.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.hidden.src: The standard hidden-stem table (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.nayin.title: Na Yin 纳音
pg.bazi.pro.ex.nayin.what: A poetic name for each of the sixty stem-and-branch pairs, two pairs sharing each of thirty names, such as 路旁土 'earth by the roadside'. Each name carries an element of its own.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.nayin.how: Looked up from the sixty-pair table.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.nayin.src: 三命通會, on Na Yin (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stage.title: Life stage 星运 (十二长生)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stage.what: A cycle of twelve stages, from birth through growth and peak to rest and renewal, applied to the Day Master in each branch. The names are traditional labels for phases of a cycle, not predictions.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stage.how: Each stem begins its cycle in a fixed branch; Yang stems count forward through the branches and Yin stems count backward.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stage.src: 三命通會, on the twelve stages (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.self.title: Self-seated stage 自坐
pg.bazi.pro.ex.self.what: The same twelve-stage cycle, but for each pillar's own stem sitting on its own branch.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.self.how: As for the life stage, using the pillar's own stem instead of the Day Master.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.self.src: 三命通會, on the twelve stages
pg.bazi.pro.ex.xunkong.title: Empty branches 空亡
pg.bazi.pro.ex.xunkong.what: The sixty pairs run in six groups of ten (旬). Twelve branches meet only ten stems in a group, so two branches are left without a stem: they are called empty for every pillar in that group.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.xunkong.how: Find the group the pillar belongs to; the two branches it leaves out are its empty branches.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.xunkong.src: The classical 旬空 rule (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stars.title: Auxiliary stars 神煞
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stars.what: Named markers looked up from the stems and branches. Fate Tutor shows only a small, neutral set and leaves out every star linked with loss, harm to health or the end of life.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stars.how: Each star has a lookup table, counted from the day stem, the year stem, the year or day branch, or the month branch, as noted on the star.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.stars.src: 三命通會 (四庫全書本), 卷02, 卷03, 卷05; 天德 completed from 星學大成 卷01 by the same author
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palace.title: Palace 宫位
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palace.what: Tradition links each pillar with a circle of people and a period of life: the year with ancestors and early years, the month with parents and youth, the day with oneself and one's partner, the hour with children and later years.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.luck.title: Ten-year luck cycle 大运
pg.bazi.pro.ex.luck.what: From an age worked out at birth, the chart is read together with a new pillar every ten years. The pillars follow the month pillar forward or backward through the sixty pairs.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.luck.how: Forward for a man born in a Yang year or a woman born in a Yin year, otherwise backward. The starting age counts three days to the nearest solar term as one year of life.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.luck.src: 淵海子平, on the luck cycles (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.flow.title: Year and month pillars 流年 · 流月
pg.bazi.pro.ex.flow.what: Every year and every month has its own pillar. Tradition reads them against the birth chart and the current luck cycle.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.flow.how: A year's pillar comes from the sixty-year cycle and starts at Start of Spring; a month's pillar starts at its solar term, with its stem from the year stem (Five Tigers rule).
pg.bazi.pro.ex.flow.src: Classical calendar rules (checked against the lunar_python reference library)
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palaces.title: Destiny palace, body palace, conception pillar
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palaces.what: Three extra pillars some schools add to the chart: the destiny palace (命宫) and body palace (身宫) from the birth month and hour, and the conception pillar (胎元) from the birth month.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palaces.how: 命宫 and 身宫 count from the month and hour branches, with the stem from the year stem; 胎元 is the month stem one step on and the month branch three steps on.
pg.bazi.pro.ex.palaces.src: Classical rules (checked against the lunar_python reference library)

pg.bazi.pro.ex.rel.what: Classical names for how two or three characters meet: combinations (合), clashes (冲), seasonal groups (会), punishments (刑), harms (害) and breaks (破). They are named patterns, not events.

pg.liuren.three.title: Three transmissions (三傳)
pg.liuren.how.title: How the first transmission was chosen
pg.liuren.step.plate: The month general {g} ({name}) is placed on the hour {h}; every heaven branch moves {s} places from its earth branch.
pg.liuren.step.lessons: The day stem {stem} lodges in {lodge}; with the day branch {branch} this gives the four lessons.
pg.liuren.step.bubei: One lesson repeats another, so only three count (不備). On a yin day the book counts from the day branch:
pg.liuren.step.bubei_yang: One lesson repeats another, so only three count (不備). On a yang day the book counts from the day stem:
pg.liuren.cand.alike: , same yin or yang as the day
pg.liuren.cand.depth: , {d} places on its way home, seat {c}
pg.liuren.step.middle.heaven: Middle and last: each is the heaven branch standing on the one before.
pg.liuren.step.middle.punish: Middle and last come by punishment (刑), or by clash (沖) where the punishment stops, as 伏吟 asks.
pg.liuren.step.middle.fixed: Middle and last are taken from the lessons, as this way prescribes.
pg.liuren.way.yuanshou: 元首: no lower strikes upper, and exactly one upper strikes lower; that upper is the first transmission.
pg.liuren.way.chongshen: 重審: exactly one lower strikes upper, and the book takes it before any upper strike.
pg.liuren.way.zhiyi: 知一 (比用): several strikes of the same kind; the one whose branch matches the day's yin or yang is taken.
pg.liuren.way.shehai: 涉害: the strikes are all alike (or none alike) with the day, so each is walked home along the earth plate, counting the places that strike it the same way; the deepest is taken.
pg.liuren.way.jianji: 見機: the walk home gives a tie, so the one standing on a 孟 seat (寅申巳亥) is taken.
pg.liuren.way.chawei: 察微: the walk home gives a tie and none stands on a 孟 seat, so the one on a 仲 seat (子午卯酉) is taken.
pg.liuren.way.zhuixia: 綴瑕: still a tie, so a yang day takes the one first seen on the day side, a yin day on the branch side.
pg.liuren.way.haoshi: 蒿矢 (遙克): no lesson has a strike, so a branch in lessons 2 to 4 that strikes the day stem from afar is taken.
pg.liuren.way.danshe: 彈射 (遙克): no lesson has a strike and nothing strikes the day stem, so a branch the day stem strikes from afar is taken.
pg.liuren.way.hushi: 虎視轉蓬 (昴星): no strike near or far on a yang day, so the heaven branch standing on 酉 is taken; then the branch's upper, then the day's upper.
pg.liuren.way.dongshe: 冬蛇掩目 (昴星): no strike near or far on a yin day, so the earth branch under heaven's 酉 is taken; then the day's upper, then the branch's upper.
pg.liuren.way.biezhe: 別責: only three lessons and no strike, so a yang day takes the branch over its partner stem's house, a yin day the next branch of its triad; middle and last are the day's upper.
pg.liuren.way.bazhuan: 八專: day stem and branch share a house and the two lessons have no strike (distant strikes are not used), so the book counts three places from the day's upper, forward on a yang day, back from the branch's upper on a yin day.
pg.liuren.way.fuyin_ziren: 伏吟 自任: heaven sits on earth unmoved and there is no strike; a yang day starts from the day's own house.
pg.liuren.way.fuyin_zixin: 伏吟 自信: heaven sits on earth unmoved and there is no strike; a yin day starts from the day branch.
pg.liuren.way.fuyin_duchuan: 伏吟 杜傳: heaven sits on earth unmoved and the chain of punishments is blocked, so the book switches between day and branch, or takes the clash.
pg.liuren.way.fuyin_ke: 伏吟 with a strike: heaven sits on earth unmoved, but the day stem and its house strike, so that lesson starts the chain.
pg.liuren.way.jinglan: 返吟 井欄射: every branch faces its opposite and no lesson has a strike, so an 丑 day takes the branch over 巳, a 未 day the branch over 亥; then the branch's upper, then the day's upper.
pg.liuren.way.fanyin: This is a 返吟 chart (every branch faces its opposite); with a strike it is read the usual way.
pg.liuren.way.bazhuan_day: Day stem and branch share a house (八專 day), so only two lessons are distinct.
pg.liuren.legend.title: Reading the chart
pg.liuren.legend.p1: The earth plate never moves; the heaven plate turns so that the month general sits on the hour. Every fact below is read off where heaven meets earth.
pg.liuren.legend.p2: The twelve generals (天將) ride the heaven plate, led by the noble. Their English names here are plain glosses of the Chinese.
pg.liuren.legend.p3: 旬空 are the two branches the day's ten-day week leaves out; a transmission on one of them is marked empty.
pg.liuren.not_forecast: These are the facts the book reads from. Fate Tutor does not turn them into a forecast.
pg.liuren.left.title: What this page leaves out, and why
pg.liuren.left.p1: The asker's birth year and running year (本命, 行年), the hidden stems (遁干), the many spirit stars (神煞) and the book's readings of each chart type are not shown. They turn the facts into judgements, and some touch topics Fate Tutor does not cover.
pg.liuren.left.p2: The noble star follows the book's verse. The 1781 editors of the 四庫全書 noted that it keeps a common order, not the one they preferred:
pg.liuren.left.p3: Where the book disagrees with itself, the page follows the stated rule: one worked example in 卷九 starts 庚辰日 午時辰將 from 午, but the depth rule of 卷七 gives 寅.
pg.liuren.source.title: 六壬大全
pg.liuren.source.p1: All rules come from 六壬大全, a Ming handbook in twelve volumes with no author named, kept in the 1781 四庫全書 and public domain on Chinese Wikisource. 卷一 gives the rules for building the chart, 卷二 the month generals and the twelve generals, 卷四 the noble verse, and 卷七 the worked charts for each way of choosing the first transmission.
pg.liuren.source.p2: Checked against the book: the engine gives the book's own worked charts, and over all 720 charts it gives the counts the book states (16 昴星, the nine 別責 days it names, one 獨足, six 井欄 days). The online copy has a few slips, such as 大雪 for 小雪 at the 寅 general; our checker names each one.
pg.liuren.about.title: One of the three classical methods
pg.liuren.about.p1: Da Liu Ren, with 奇門遁甲 and 太乙, makes up the three classical methods (三式). It is a chart of the moment a question is asked, built only from the day, the hour and the Sun's place among the solar terms.
pg.liuren.about.p2: Fate Tutor lays out the chart and shows its sources. It does not turn a chart into a forecast, financial advice, medical advice or a decision made for you.

pg.qimen.board.title: The nine palaces (九宮)
pg.qimen.board.note: Laid out as the book draws it, south at the top. In each palace: the god, the star with the stem it carries (heaven plate), the door, and the earth-plate stem at the foot.
pg.qimen.board.center: Middle palace: its stem travels with the star of 坤.
pg.qimen.legend.title: Reading the chart
pg.qimen.legend.p1: The earth plate stays put for the five days of the 元. Each hour the stars turn as one ring onto the hour stem, the doors turn as another ring counted by the hour, and the gods follow the chief star.
pg.qimen.legend.p2: Stars, doors and gods are shown by their Chinese names with pinyin. Fate Tutor does not translate or explain them as good or bad.
pg.qimen.not_forecast: These are the facts the books read from. Fate Tutor does not turn them into a forecast.
pg.qimen.left.title: What this page leaves out, and why
pg.qimen.left.p1: The named patterns (格局), the readings of stars, doors and gods, the birth year and running year, and the charms and spells in the books are not shown: they turn the chart into judgements or rituals. Year, month and day charts are not set either; this page sets the hour chart.
pg.qimen.left.p2: The modern split-and-fill method (拆補) is shown only as a switch. The Qing imperial 御定奇門寶鑑 rejects it:
pg.qimen.left.p3: The books disagree on how far the 局 may run ahead before the leap; the page uses nine days counting both ends, as in 統宗's dated example for 1718, and the checker repeats that example.
pg.qimen.source.title: 煙波釣叟歌, 遁甲演義 and 奇門遁甲統宗
pg.qimen.source.p1: The core verse 煙波釣叟歌 (Song, revised in the Ming) gives the turning of the plate. 遁甲演義 (程道生, Ming, in the 四庫全書) gives the 局 for each term, the leap rule and two worked charts; 奇門遁甲統宗 (Ming) gives the same verse and a dated leap run for 1717 to 1719. All are public domain on Chinese Wikisource; 御定奇門寶鑑 (Qing) was read as a further witness.
pg.qimen.source.p2: Checked against the books: the engine gives both worked charts of 遁甲演義 and 統宗's dated leap of 1718, and all 1,080 plates agree with a second version built from the books' tables. The online copies have a few slips, such as 八五二 for 八二五 at 小暑; our checker names each one.
pg.qimen.about.title: One of the three classical methods
pg.qimen.about.p1: Qi Men Dun Jia, with 大六壬 and 太乙, makes up the three classical methods (三式). The hour chart is built only from the solar term, the day and the hour.
pg.qimen.about.p2: Fate Tutor sets the chart and shows its sources. It does not turn a chart into a forecast, financial advice, medical advice or a decision made for you.

pg.qizheng.title: Seven Governors and Four Remainders: Your Birth Sky
pg.qizheng.lead: Chinese star astrology reads the Sun, Moon and five planets (七政) with four computed points (四餘) against twelve palaces and 28 lunar mansions. This page sets them out by the Qing court calendar (時憲曆) as 清史稿 records it: the real sky, and the court's own rules for the four remainders.

pg.qizheng.legend.title: Reading the sky
pg.qizheng.legend.p1: The palaces follow the Sun's year (they are the same twelve sections as the Western signs). The mansions follow the stars, so they slowly slide against the palaces: today they sit about 4° further on than in 1744.
pg.qizheng.legend.p2: The Sun, Moon and planets are where astronomy puts them. 月孛, 羅㬋 and 計都 are the Qing court's corrected lunar apogee and nodes; 紫氣 has no body in the sky and follows its own fixed rate.
pg.qizheng.not_forecast: These are the facts the tradition reads from. Fate Tutor does not turn them into a forecast.
pg.qizheng.left.title: What this page leaves out, and why
pg.qizheng.left.p1: The transforming stars (化曜), the many spirit stars (神煞), the periods of life (限度) and the books' readings are not shown: they turn the sky into judgements, and some touch topics Fate Tutor does not cover.
pg.qizheng.left.p2: The older Ming handbooks (張果星宗, 星學大成) print fixed tables of their own era; this page follows the later Qing court method instead. 清史稿 records how the remainders were defined and renamed:
pg.qizheng.left.p3: Twelve of the 28 marker stars are fixed by 清史稿's own 1744 positions, and the catalogue matches them within 3′. For 心 the page uses the mansion's first star (σ Sco); some modern lists use Antares instead.
pg.qizheng.source.title: 清史稿, 星學大成 and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue
pg.qizheng.source.p1: The palaces, the mansion method and the four remainders come from the calendar treatise of 清史稿 (chapters 45, 48, 50) and its astronomy chapter (28). The life palace and the twelve palace roles come from 星學大成 (萬民英, 1563). The 28 marker stars come from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue. All are public domain.
pg.qizheng.source.p2: Checked: the stars carried back to 1744 match 清史稿's printed positions within 3′; the planets agree with an independent ephemeris within a few arcseconds; the remainders are rebuilt from the constants read out of 清史稿 and agree within a second of arc.
pg.qizheng.about.title: Chinese star astrology
pg.qizheng.about.p1: Qi Zheng Si Yu grew from the Tang and Song dynasties and flourished in the Ming. It reads the actual sky at birth, divided by palaces and by the 28 lunar mansions of Chinese astronomy.
pg.qizheng.about.p2: Fate Tutor sets out the sky and shows its sources. It does not turn a chart into a forecast, financial advice, medical advice or a decision made for you.

pg.ziwei.legend.daxian: Ten-year periods (大限) follow the book's 安大限訣. Ages are counted the Chinese way, 1 at birth; the first period begins at the bureau's number, from 水二局 at 2 to 火六局 at 6.
pg.ziwei.quote.daxian: 「阳男阴女从命前一宫起顺行」
pg.ziwei.quote.daxian2: 「阴男阳女从命后一宫起逆行」
pg.ziwei.legend.daxian.other: Other books differ. The Daoist-canon text 紫微斗數 starts them at 命 itself (or at 申 for 陰男陽女), and many charts made today also start at 命, so a chart from elsewhere may show different periods. This page follows 紫微斗數全書.
